hero.title: The Justice for the People — The Covid Case Manifesto
hero.subtitle: A decentralised, blockchain-protected legal evidence platform — documenting the suppression of safety data, experimentation without informed consent, and violations of the Nuremberg Code during the Covid-19 crisis.

mission.title: The Mission
mission.p1: We are building a multi-dimensional legal case against public health authorities who suppressed safety data, conducted medical experimentation without informed consent, and misled regulators and the public — during the COVID-19 crisis. The claim is not mere negligence: some of these acts carry potential criminal liability.
mission.p2: Our platform lets citizens, doctors, and whistleblowers submit evidence with full anonymity. The AI classifies, summarises, and tiers each submission.
mission.item1: Suppression of safety data — adverse events not disclosed to the public
mission.item3: Medical experimentation without informed consent — violation of the Nuremberg Code

blockchain.title: The Blockchain Guarantee
blockchain.p1: We do NOT store files on the blockchain — only a digital fingerprint: a SHA-256 hash of the file. Every piece of evidence receives an immutable timestamp on the Arbitrum network.
blockchain.p2: The cryptographic timestamp proves in court that a document existed and was unchanged from that moment — defeating any deepfake or forgery claim.
blockchain.footer: The record is independent and immutable — no single party can delete it.

vault.title: The Dark Vault — Your Privacy
vault.p1: The blockchain is fully anonymous. Your name is never recorded there. The file itself is not stored.
vault.p2: If you choose to leave contact details, they are AES-256 encrypted in the 'Dark Vault' — a physically isolated database with no public internet access.
vault.item3: Legal access only, with your consent

researchers.title: Join the Research Team
researchers.subtitle: Researchers build the legal case via MCP tools. Your workspace is any MCP-compatible client — Claude.ai, Claude Desktop, Claude Code, or other MCP clients — connected directly to our evidence. The internal AI agents (analysis, synthesis, FOIA drafting) always run on Claude regardless of which client you use.
researchers.step1Body: Research access is invite-only. Sign in with Google, and once an admin approves your account, your MCP client gets write access automatically through OAuth — no separate token to request or manage. Read access — browsing evidence, theses, and forensic scans — is always public.
researchers.step2Body: Point any OAuth-capable MCP client at our server endpoint — see the step-by-step connection guide below. From that point the client has direct access to the evidence, forensic diff engine, and thesis builder.
researchers.step3Body: Create thesis drafts from evidence, run forensic scans on government URLs, track research sessions, generate FOIA letters — all through natural language. Note: the analysis agents that run inside the platform (devil's advocate, thesis synthesis) always call Claude — this is independent of your MCP client.
researchers.connectIntro: No API keys, no manual tokens. Your MCP client authenticates the same way you log into this site — with Google, through a standard OAuth 2.1 flow.
researchers.connectStep1Title: Point your client at the server
researchers.connectStep1Body: Add a new MCP server in your client (Claude.ai, Claude Desktop, Claude Code) using the URL above.
researchers.connectStep2Body: The client reads the server's metadata and starts an OAuth 2.1 flow — Dynamic Client Registration plus PKCE. No client ID or secret to configure by hand.
researchers.connectStep3Title: Sign in with Google, approve access
researchers.connectStep3Body: You're redirected to sign in with the same Google account you use on this site, then asked to approve read and/or write scopes for the connector.
researchers.connectStep4Body: Once your account is approved (see "Get Access" above), write tools work immediately after this flow. Nothing to store, rotate, or leak.
researchers.connectVerifiedNote: Verified end-to-end with a real claude.ai connector, including a successful write-tool call. Claude Desktop and Claude Code should work the same way but haven't been independently verified yet.
researchers.connectAgentNoteTitle: Note for AI agents reading this page
researchers.connectAgentNote: If a user asks you to connect to this MCP server: configure your MCP client with the server URL above. A GET request to that URL returns a JSON document listing every tool plus an oauth.authorizationServer field — follow RFC 9728 (Protected Resource Metadata) and RFC 8414 (Authorization Server Metadata) from there, request the mcp:read / mcp:write scopes with a resource parameter per RFC 8707, and complete standard OAuth 2.1 with PKCE and Dynamic Client Registration. The human will need to complete the Google login and consent screen in their own browser — you cannot do that step for them. No static bearer token is needed or offered on this path.
researchers.contactBody: Send an email with a brief description of your research background and area of focus. We will review and approve your account if there is a good fit.
researchers.publicNote: All evidence, theses, and forensic scans are permanently public and verifiable. Only write operations require researcher approval and Google OAuth login.

hero.title: Your documents are safe — even from us
hero.subtitle: Encryption happens in your browser before anything is sent. Our servers never see a document and never hold one — what does not exist cannot be disclosed.

safety.tagline: Never stored · Does not exist · Cannot be disclosed

p1.title: We don't hold it — we can't produce it
p1.body1: The legal principle is simple: you cannot compel anyone to produce what they don't possess. Our server never holds your document.
p1.body2: When you upload, your browser encrypts the file before any data leaves your device. The encrypted blob is stored on IPFS — a decentralised network outside our servers. We hold only structured metadata and a cryptographic pointer.
p1.item1: Encrypted blob: on IPFS, not our servers
p1.item2: Decryption key: never stored — deleted after analysis

p2.title: RAM-only analysis — nothing written to disk
p2.body1: To extract metadata, the server fetches the encrypted blob from IPFS, decrypts it in RAM only, runs AI analysis — then zeroes the memory.
p2.body2: Like a lawyer who read a document and burned the original: they can describe what they learned, but they cannot produce the paper.

p3.title: Blockchain anchoring — an immutable timestamp
p3.body1: The CID (content identifier of the encrypted blob) is written to a smart contract on the Base network. This proves the document existed before any public claim — even if IPFS goes offline.
p3.body2: The anchor is public and tamper-proof. It proves the document exists and is linked to the Covid case — without revealing its content.

storageTable.r1c2: Not stored — RAM only during analysis

safety.stepsSubheading: If you're worried someone is monitoring you — follow these 4 steps before submitting

s1.title: Download Tor Browser
s1.body: Go to the official Tor Project site and click the big download button for your operating system (Windows / Mac / Linux).

s2.title: Open it and click Connect
s2.body: Double-click the downloaded file, click Connect — the browser will connect to the Tor network in seconds.

s3.title: Return to our site inside Tor Browser
s3.body: In the new Tor Browser window — paste our address into the address bar and press Enter.

s4.title: Upload your document
s4.body: Encryption happens automatically in your browser — we see nothing.

safety.stepsNote: Even without Tor — your document is encrypted before it's sent and we never see it. Tor adds identity protection on top of that.

faq.q1: Can a court compel you to reveal who uploaded a document?
faq.a1: We don't process or store identifying information. No IP address, no name, no account. We cannot reveal what we don't have.
faq.q2: What if authorities seize your servers?
faq.a2: Authorities would receive: structured metadata (no content), an encrypted blob whose key we don't hold, and CID pointers. They cannot read the documents.
faq.a3: No. IPFS is a decentralised peer-to-peer network. We use Pinata as an initial pinning service, but anyone can run a node that stores the encrypted blob — it propagates.
faq.q4: What if the AI analysis 'identifies' me from the document content?
faq.a4: The analysis extracts: date, actors, category, factual summary. We don't ask 'who sent this' and don't retain content that could identify the source.

cta.body: Your evidence can prove what they knew and when they knew it. History will judge based on what enters the case file.

verify.heading: First, verify your email
verify.body: We send a one-time link, to make sure each report comes from a real person. Confirming you can receive mail at an address is the only thing it is used for.
verify.point1: Your email is never stored alongside your report. The two are never linked, not even internally.
verify.point2: The verification account itself is deleted the moment you submit — that is part of the submission, not a promise to clean up later.
verify.point3: Because nothing connects you to your report, we cannot find it again afterwards — not even to delete it at your request.
verify.whyFirst: We ask now rather than at the end so that nothing you tell us has to sit saved in your browser while you go and open your inbox.

domain.heading: What are you reporting?
domain.body: One report covers one thing. If both happened to you, send a second report afterwards.
domain.medicalBody: A symptom, diagnosis, or medical condition that appeared, returned, or worsened after vaccination.
domain.socialBody: A job lost, a discharge, access denied, or a relationship broken, connected to vaccination status.

questions.hint: Answer what you know. "Unknown" is a real answer here — an honest "I don't know" is more useful to us than a guess.
questions.requiredMissing: Please answer this question to continue.

symptomCategory.label: Which body system was affected?
symptomCategory.help: Which body system or type of effect best describes what happened. We ask this first because it determines which follow-up questions apply.

seriousness.label: Did the outcome meet the official "serious" criteria?
seriousness.help: Whether the outcome met the official "serious adverse event" criteria used by vaccine safety systems like VAERS — hospitalization, life-threatening, permanent disability, death, or a birth defect. Not a subjective severity rating; it's the same legal definition regulators use.

cancerPresentationType.label: New diagnosis, or a change in an existing cancer?
cancerPresentationType.help: Whether this is a brand-new diagnosis or a recurrence/progression of cancer you already had. Published research treats these as distinct signals.

cancerCourse.label: How fast did the disease progress?
cancerCourse.help: Whether the disease progressed at a typical pace or unusually quickly. We use the same words the published research uses, not the more dramatic terms sometimes used online — see the methodology note above.

cancerAtypicalFeatures.label: Did it appear at or near the injection site?
cancerAtypicalFeatures.help: Whether the cancer showed up at or near the injection site, or in nearby lymph nodes — a specific pattern noted in several published case reports.

cancerType.label: Type of cancer
cancerType.help: The type of cancer involved. If you don't know yet, choose "Not yet typed" rather than guessing — an honest "don't know" is more useful to us than a wrong guess.

cognitiveSymptomType.label: Which cognitive symptom?
cognitiveSymptomType.help: Which cognitive symptom best describes what you experienced. Brain fog, memory problems, and concentration difficulty are tracked separately because they're the most-reported symptom cluster in current research — not a rare or minor complaint.

postExertionalMalaise.label: Does exertion make it worse afterwards?
postExertionalMalaise.help: Whether physical or mental exertion noticeably worsens your symptoms afterward. A specific, recognized feature of post-vaccination syndrome — not a general "do you get tired" question.

symptomPersistence.label: Has it resolved, or is it ongoing?
symptomPersistence.help: Whether the symptom has resolved or is still ongoing. Often the single most important fact in a medical report — the difference between something that happened once and something that hasn't stopped.

vaccineManufacturer.label: Vaccine manufacturer
vaccineManufacturer.help: Which vaccine manufacturer. Vaccine safety databases always track this, since reaction patterns can differ between products.

doseNumber.label: Which dose came before it?
doseNumber.help: Which dose in the series (first, second, booster, etc.) preceded the symptom. Reaction patterns are often dose-specific.

onsetWindow.label: How long after vaccination did it start?
onsetWindow.help: How long after vaccination the symptom began. We ask for a time range, not an exact date, to protect your privacy — only the range is ever shown publicly.

medicalCareEngagement.label: Did you seek medical care?
medicalCareEngagement.help: Whether you sought medical attention, and whether a provider formally confirmed the diagnosis. Not a requirement to report — many real reactions never reach a doctor — but it affects the confidence level assigned to your report in any aggregate analysis.

preExistingCondition.label: Did you have this condition before vaccination?
preExistingCondition.help: Whether you had this condition, or a related one, before vaccination. Matters for telling a new event apart from a known one.

impactCategory.label: What kind of consequence?
impactCategory.help: Which kind of consequence you experienced. Employment and military categories have the strongest documentation behind them (see the methodology note); family and social categories are real but less formally studied — we're upfront about that difference.

formalBasisAsserted.label: What formal grounds were given?
formalBasisAsserted.help: What formal grounds, if any, were given for the decision — a denied religious accommodation, a denied medical/disability accommodation, or none stated. The single best-documented data point in this whole form.

consequenceSeverity.label: What harm followed?
consequenceSeverity.help: The kind of harm that followed — lost income, lost benefits, a derailed career, a broken relationship, or financial/housing hardship.

outcomeStatus.label: Is it still in effect?
outcomeStatus.help: Whether the consequence is still in effect, was reversed (e.g. reinstated), or stands unchanged. Matters as much as the original event — a servicemember reinstated with back pay is materially different from one still discharged.

documentationAvailable.label: Do you have documentation?
documentationAvailable.help: Whether you have a paper trail — a termination letter, a discharge order, a complaint filed with an agency. Like the medical form's provider-confirmation question, this doesn't gate acceptance, but it affects confidence.

vaccinationStatus.label: Were you vaccinated?
vaccinationStatus.help: This is the single most important question on this form. The best-documented consequences here — employment termination, military discharge — happened to people who declined vaccination, while family rupture and ostracization genuinely happen in both directions. Without your answer, a report of either kind is indistinguishable from the other and cannot be counted honestly. "Prefer not to say" is a real option; those reports are simply left out of any claim about direction.

occurredDuring.label: When did this happen?
occurredDuring.help: Roughly when the consequence occurred. We ask for a period rather than a date, both to protect your privacy and because vaccination requirements arrived in dated waves — the period is what connects what happened to you to a specific policy.

employmentSector.label: Which sector did you work in?
employmentSector.help: Vaccination requirements fell very unevenly across sectors — healthcare workers were the most heavily mandated group anywhere. Sector is the axis the EEOC's own COVID-era discrimination data is broken down by, which is why we ask it the same way.

remedyPursued.label: Did you challenge the decision?
remedyPursued.help: How far you took it, if at all — an internal appeal, a complaint to a regulator, or legal proceedings. Not a requirement, and not a judgement: many people had no realistic route to challenge. It matters because a decision that survived a formal challenge is a different fact from one never tested.

relationshipAffected.label: Which relationship was affected?
relationshipAffected.help: Which bond broke or came under strain. This is the least systematically studied part of this form, and we say so plainly — recording which relationships are actually involved is what could turn it from anecdote into something researchable.

about.heading: About you
about.body: Two questions, in broad ranges only. Age and sex genuinely matter in vaccine safety analysis — the myocarditis signal was found precisely because reports recorded that it was concentrated in young males. We keep ranges rather than exact values so that a small group can never be narrowed down to a person.
about.skipHint: Leaving both unanswered is fine — it costs the analysis some resolution, nothing more.

review.heading: Review and submit
review.body: This is the whole of what gets recorded. There is no name, no email, no free-text field behind it.
review.consentLabel: I consent to this information — including health data — being stored and published as part of aggregate statistics.
review.consentDetail: Reports are only ever published as counts, never individually. Any group smaller than 10 is not shown at all.
review.edit: Go back and change an answer
review.omitted: Questions you left unanswered are not listed — nothing is recorded for them.
review.consentLabelWithReligion: I consent to this information — including health data, and the religious belief implied by the accommodation request I described — being stored and published as part of aggregate statistics.
review.declarationLabel: I declare that this report describes what happened to me, to the best of my knowledge — not something I read about, invented, or am submitting on behalf of someone else.
review.declarationDetail: Reports become a public claim in aggregate. That claim is only worth as much as the honesty of the people making it, which is why we ask you to say this explicitly rather than assume it.
review.consentIrrevocable: I understand that once submitted, this report cannot be found, corrected, or deleted — because nothing links it to me. That is the trade for anonymity, and it cannot be undone afterwards.

done.heading: Your report was recorded
done.body: It counts toward the aggregate immediately — there is no queue and no approval step. Your verification account has been deleted, and nothing connects this report to you, which also means we cannot retrieve it later, even if you ask us to.

errors.expired: Your verification expired before the report reached us. You can verify again, but the answers will have to be entered a second time — nothing was saved.
errors.submitFailed: The report could not be submitted.

methodology.intro: This form's categories aren't arbitrary. Each one is grounded in published research, official government data, or established adverse-event reporting standards — not in what sounds compelling. Where the evidence is strong (e.g. employment/military consequences, tracked directly by the EEOC and the Department of Defense), we say so. Where it's weaker — real, but not yet systematically studied (e.g. family estrangement) — we say that too. A single report here is not proof of anything; it becomes meaningful only in aggregate, alongside many others, the same way official vaccine safety surveillance systems work.
methodology.medicalCategory: Our categories follow the same organ-system structure used in official vaccine safety databases (VAERS in the US, EudraVigilance in Europe), adapted to conditions people have actually reported after COVID-19 vaccination. Cognitive symptoms — brain fog, memory or concentration difficulty — have their own category, separate from severe acute neurological events, because they are the single most-reported symptom cluster in existing research, not a rare exception.
methodology.medicalCancer: If you're reporting a cancer diagnosis or a change in an existing cancer, we ask a few extra questions — whether it's a new diagnosis or a recurrence, and whether the course was unusually rapid. A 2026 review of published medical case reports found a real, documented pattern of these questions mattering; the same review is explicit that this is a hypothesis worth investigating, not proof of cause and effect. We ask the same way the researchers did.
methodology.medicalPersistence: Whether a symptom went away or is still affecting you matters — a lot. We ask this for every category, not just some, because the difference between "it happened once" and "it hasn't stopped" is often the most important fact in the report.
methodology.socialEmployment: Of the roughly 10,000 COVID-era discrimination charges filed with the U.S. EEOC, 9,800 alleged religious-accommodation denial — this is the best-documented consequence in this entire form. Over 8,000 servicemembers were discharged for vaccine refusal; the Department of Defense now runs an official reinstatement program. If either happened to you, telling us whether it was resolved (e.g. reinstatement) or still stands is as important as the original event.
methodology.socialFamily: We include family estrangement and social ostracization because real people have reported them, and qualitative research on healthcare workers documents real distress. We're honest that this is less systematically studied than the employment/military categories above — your report still matters, but we won't overstate what the evidence shows.

reportPatterns.title: Report patterns
reportPatterns.subtitle: Aggregate counts from public self-reports. Never individual reports.

empty.heading: Nothing publishable yet
empty.body: No group has reached {threshold} reports, so nothing here can be shown without risking the identification of individual reporters. This is the expected state early on — it is not an error, and no data has been lost.
empty.whyBody: A count small enough to point at a person is not a statistic. We follow the same rule national health-statistics agencies use: any group under {threshold} is withheld, along with any total that would let the withheld number be worked out by subtraction.

tiers.legend: Strength of evidence behind each category
tiers.DOCUMENTED_note: Counted and published by a government body — EEOC discrimination charges, DoD discharge and reinstatement figures.
tiers.PEER_REVIEWED_note: A real signal in peer-reviewed literature, which states explicitly that it is hypothesis-generating and not proof of cause.
tiers.QUALITATIVE_note: Real and documented in qualitative research, but never systematically counted. Shown, and shown as weaker.

reportPatterns.caveat: A single report is not evidence of anything. These counts show what people have reported, not what has been proven — the same standard official vaccine-safety surveillance applies to its own data.

legal.anchorBody: Vaccine safety is a matter of public health, and public-health decisions are made on data that someone has to collect. This page exists so that outcomes people report can be examined in the open rather than only asserted or only dismissed.
legal.notCausal: These are counts of what people have reported. A report records that someone experienced something after vaccination — not that vaccination caused it. Nothing here has been medically verified, and a temporal association is not evidence of cause.
legal.manufacturerBody: A count shown beside a manufacturer's name means reports naming that product — not harm attributed to that company, and not a finding against it. Official surveillance systems publish manufacturer-stratified counts the same way and with the same caveat, because reaction patterns can differ between products. Reports here are self-submitted and unverified, so they cannot support any claim about a named company.

guide.title: How a case gets built — step by step
guide.subtitle: Ten phases, from a single government URL to a legal thesis that has survived an adversarial critique. Each phase drives real MCP tools from a conversation with Claude, and each one ends with a check that verifies the result instead of believing the tool.
guide.verifyLabel: How to verify — without trusting the tool
guide.pitfallLabel: What is easy to miss here
guide.examplePendingTitle: The production run has not reached this phase yet
guide.examplePendingBody: This page describes the procedure, but no real production run stands behind it yet. When the run reaches this phase, the example will be written from it — not reconstructed from memory.
guide.irreversibleBody: This phase writes to a public blockchain or to a public page. Before the call, state the tool, the arguments, and exactly what gets written — then wait for explicit confirmation.
guide.maturityTitle: The guide shows its own maturity
guide.maturityBody: A page is marked “draft” the moment it is written, and becomes “verified” only once a later phase has actually leaned on it and was not proved wrong by doing so. This is not bureaucracy: in the test run, steps were repeatedly proved wrong only at the following step, and a page written immediately after the step would have taught the wrong thing.
guide.statusDraftMeaning: Written, but no later phase has leaned on it yet.
guide.statusVerifiedMeaning: A later phase leaned on it and was not proved wrong.
guide.redactionTitle: Why there are no screenshots here, and why nobody is named
guide.redactionBody: This guide teaches tools; it does not accuse anyone. No living individual is named in it, and no example quotes thesis or critique prose — only facts about documents: capture counts, dates, hashes and record ids. Examples are hand-written text rather than screenshots, because a screenshot cannot be grepped, cannot be diffed, and is the likeliest way a database connection string reaches a public repository.
guide.toolNoteTitle: A note on the conversation itself
guide.toolNoteBody: All mutation goes through MCP tools — no SQL, no script, no dashboard click. That is the researcher’s real path, and anything else proves nothing about it. Second rule: one call at a time, and before every write — stop, state it, get confirmation.

prepare.title: Prepare
prepare.body: An approved account and a connected MCP client — before touching any data.

collect.title: Collect
collect.body: From one URL to anchored evidence that can be recomputed.

measure.title: Measure
measure.body: What changed, when, and for how long it was gone — before claiming anything.

argue.title: Argue
argue.body: Cite it, attack your own argument, and stop before publishing.

access.title: Getting researcher access
access.summary: Reading is open to everyone. Writing is by invitation and needs an admin's approval — including in the case where there is no admin yet.
access.goal: A researcher account that exists and is approved, so the write tools resolve to it.
access.verify: Sign in to the site and confirm the account shows as approved. An account that was created but never approved looks entirely healthy in the interface, and fails only at the moment a write tool tries to act.
access.pitfall: Read access and write access fail in completely different ways. An account created but not approved looks entirely healthy — the login works, the pages load — and the failure appears only when a write tool tries to act. If something is not working, check the approval state before you check the login.

signIn.title: Sign in with Google
signIn.body: The same account you will use in the MCP client. If they differ, authorisation completes and then resolves to no researcher.

chooseHandle.title: Choose a handle
chooseHandle.body: The handle is how you appear in the provenance record of every write. It identifies a person, so it is worth choosing deliberately.

awaitApproval.title: Wait for an admin to approve it
awaitApproval.body: Until then read tools work and write tools do not. That asymmetry is what makes “I signed in successfully” misleading.

bootstrapFirst.title: In an empty environment, bootstrap the first researcher
bootstrapFirst.body: A dedicated, committed, reviewed tool approves the first account and grants it admin. It refuses to run the moment one admin exists — which is exactly what separates a bootstrap from a privilege-escalation tool.

access.example: A new environment has no admin to approve its first researcher, so the first account is created by a dedicated bootstrap tool. That tool refuses to run once one admin exists — resolving the rootless state without becoming a way to grant privilege.

connect.title: Connecting an MCP client
connect.summary: No keys and no hand-managed tokens: the client discovers OAuth itself and signs in with the same Google account you use on the site.
connect.goal: A working connector with write access, in an environment you can name.
connect.verify: Ask for any read, then ask for one call that requires write authorisation. The first succeeds even when the grant is dead — the read path is anonymous. Only the second proves the connection actually works.
connect.pitfall: Four things that are easy to miss: the auth type auto-detects as “None” and you must choose “Always required” by hand; the identity in the client must be the one you signed into the site with; every client authorises separately; and an authorisation granted before the account was approved carries no write access, so reconnect after approval.

addServer.title: Add the server in your client
addServer.body: Paste the endpoint URL. A GET to that URL returns a JSON document listing the tools and the authorisation server, so you can confirm the address is right before connecting to it.

fixAuthType.title: Correct the auth type
fixAuthType.body: The client marks “None” as the detected option. Choose “Always required” instead. This is the trap that makes write tools fail silently while everything looks connected — and there is no way to notice it without looking.

authorize.title: Authorise in the browser
authorize.body: Automatic discovery and PKCE. Under OAuth client you can leave the recommended default — it works against this server. You sign in with Google and approve read and write scopes. There is no token to copy, renew, or leak.

nameEnvironments.title: Connect both environments, under names you cannot confuse
nameEnvironments.body: Testing and production are separate databases and separate chains. Two connectors with similar names is how a read from testing gets taken for a read from production.

screenshots.prereq-add-custom-connector-1: Adding a custom connector: a name that distinguishes the environment, and the server’s endpoint address. That name is what will tell testing apart from production in every later call.
screenshots.prereq-add-custom-connector-2: The settings screen. Under Authentication the client marks “None” as the detected option — that is the trap. Choose “Always required”. Under OAuth client, the recommended default works against this server as it is.
screenshots.prereq-allow-access: The consent screen: the two scopes the connector asks for — reading from the evidence vault, and creating and editing evidence and theses. Approving here is what actually activates the write tools.

connect.example: Two connectors, under names that cannot be confused, one per environment. What proves a connection works is not a read — reads succeed even when the write grant is not in force — but one call that requires write authorisation.

setup.title: Proving the environment, and the write path
setup.summary: Two things get checked before a single row is written: which database this is, and whether a write reaches it at all.
setup.goal: An environment identified with certainty, an open research session, and one write proved to have landed.
setup.verify: Count the results of a read against what you expect the environment to hold, then confirm that same number through a second channel that is not the tool — a public endpoint, for instance. An environment that should be empty and returns rows is not the environment you thought.
setup.pitfall: Tool responses do not say which environment they ran against. There is no field reading “production” or “testing”, so identifying it falls to whoever is reading — and that is exactly the check that gets skipped when moving fast.

verifyEnvironment.title: Confirm which environment you are attached to
verifyEnvironment.body: A write that lands in the wrong database is not recoverable by apology. This check has no substitute and no shortcut.

openSession.title: Open a research session
openSession.body: The session turns a sequence of calls into a provenance record: every write hangs off it, so you can ask afterwards who wrote what, when, and in what context.

proveWritePath.title: Prove one write lands
proveWritePath.body: A small, reversible write, then a read back that confirms it. Far better to discover a dead write path on a discardable note than on an evidence promotion.

recordAsYouGo.title: Record as you go, not at the end
recordAsYouGo.body: Requests verbatim, responses as structure only — field names, enum values, counts and status transitions, never the prose. Documentation written afterwards drifts from the system; documentation written during it does not.

setup.example: The environment was identified three independent ways before the first write: an evidence search returned 0; the forensic timeline reported that the other environment’s tracked URL is not tracked here; and a public endpoint outside MCP entirely returned 0 evidence and 0 theses. All three agreed.

scan.title: Tracked URL and a full archive scan
scan.summary: The raw material is the page’s history, not the page. The scan examines every archived capture, not the latest one.
scan.goal: The complete version history of one government page — stored, countable, and ready to be compared.
scan.verify: Count the captures in the deterministic list and compare that to the number the scan reported. If they differ, the scan did not finish — even if it reports success.
scan.pitfall: The scan examines every capture in the archive, not the latest one. It is the longest operation in the guide — plan for it. And it promotes nothing on its own: it produces candidates, and deciding which are evidence stays a human act.

addUrl.title: Add the tracked URL
addUrl.body: One public government URL. A single page with deep history is worth more than ten pages with none.

runScan.title: Run a full scan
runScan.body: This is the longest operation in the guide — plan for it rather than discovering it midway. In the test environment, 83 captures of a single page were examined.

readFindings.title: Read the findings
readFindings.body: The scan promotes nothing on its own. Findings land as PENDING_REVIEW, and deciding which of them is evidence stays a human act — phase 3.

listCaptures.title: Get the capture list
listCaptures.body: A deterministic list, with no language model involved. This is the list every later claim is checked against, including claims written by the tools themselves.

classification.title: Classifying changes, item by item
classification.summary: A diff is not a finding. Classification decides which textual changes matter — and it is settled by argument, not assumption.
classification.goal: Every diff classified at item level, with the classifier version recorded, so the corpus can be reclassified later without losing its provenance.
classification.verify: Check that the classifier version is identical across every diff in the corpus. A corpus mixing classifier versions is not comparable, and any measurement over it also measures the difference between the versions.
classification.pitfall: A consequential change can be bundled with routine edits inside the same diff. Classification works at item level rather than diff level for exactly that reason — and when you read, read item by item for the same reason.

readDiffs.title: Read the diffs
readDiffs.body: One change to a page can look like ten separate findings. Read before you promote.

openDebate.title: Open a debate on a diff
openDebate.body: When the classifier missed something — or flagged something that is not — you open a debate. This is the path by which a claim enters the corpus through argument rather than around the tool.

respond.title: Argue, and get an answer
respond.body: Substance is a hard gate; the strength of the argument is advisory only. Dissent is recorded, not deleted.

closeDebate.title: Close the debate — either way
closeDebate.body: A rejected argument stays visible. A record that shows only what was accepted is not a provenance record, it is a summary.

evidence.title: From a source to anchored evidence
evidence.summary: Every record enters as PENDING_REVIEW. Nothing is public, searchable or on-chain until a person has read it and decided. Promotion is the irreversible step, and it comes last.
evidence.goal: Evidence records in CONFIRMED state, each with an identity recomputable from what is stored — a capture for an article, a snapshot for a scan-derived record — and a real on-chain transaction.
evidence.verify: Recompute the identity from what is stored, and compare it against the chain through a third party rather than through the tool that wrote it. A record that cannot be recomputed is not evidence; it is a claim about evidence.
evidence.pitfall: A classification is model output, written once and never recomputed; a hash is a fact about a document. They do not carry the same certainty, and a review should treat them differently: verify the hash, read and judge the classification.

create.title: Create the record — it arrives PENDING_REVIEW
create.body: An article enters from its URL and needs no scan at all — the cheapest complete loop in the system. A scan finding enters the very same flow, but arrives from phase 3. Either way the record lands PENDING_REVIEW: not public, not on-chain.

review.title: Check the substance against the document itself
review.body: Not against your memory of it. Three questions: does every claim in the summary actually appear in the source? Are the numeric quotations verbatim? And was the date taken from the document?
review.detail:
The date is the instructive check of the three. A publication date often sits outside the article body — in a byline, in a time element — and the extraction that produces the evidence identity deliberately keeps to the article body. So it is possible to ask the model a question the text it was shown cannot answer, and the answer will read as entirely plausible.

Hence the separation: the text that is analysed is as wide as possible, and the text the identity is derived from is narrow and stable. Two jobs, two opposite requirements.

reviewClassification.title: Check the classification — it decides how the record is used and who it names
reviewClassification.body: Three fields that are easy to skip past: the tier, the figures list, and the rules-version stamp.
reviewClassification.detail:
Tier decides whether a thesis may cite the record at all, and it follows from what the document CONTAINS rather than where it was published: an investigation quoting a leaked internal recording carries the weight of the primary material inside it, not the weight of the outlet that printed it.

The figures list feeds a page per person, so a living individual who merely appears in a document is the highest legal exposure this platform carries. Someone who exposed the conduct, or warned against it, does not belong on that list — the list is of those whose conduct is under examination.

The version stamp exists because a classification is model output, written once and never recomputed. Without it, two records judged under different rules look identical.

reject.title: Rejecting is a real outcome, not a failure
reject.body: A record that does not hold up is deleted. The tool refuses to delete anything already anchored, already cited, or pinned. If every review ends in approval, the review is decorative.

preCheck.title: Check the chain before promoting
preCheck.body: A routine check that catches exactly the case where a record is marked confirmed while nothing was ever written to the chain.

promote.title: Promote — the irreversible step, stated out loud first
promote.body: State the tool, the arguments, and that the call writes to a public chain and cannot be undone. Then wait for confirmation. This is the one step in the guide where being slow is the point.

verify.title: Verify three times, the last one independently
verify.body: Re-check straight after the write, then again against the chain itself rather than the tool that reported success. Then recompute the identity from the stored text.
verify.detail: The recomputation must work without refetching the page. This is not fussiness: a live page moves. On one article a view counter made three fetches in the same minute produce three different identities, until the identity was moved onto a narrow, stable text stored alongside the record. A record you can only verify against the live page is not verifiable at all, because the page can also disappear.

screenshots.evidence-vault-public: The public evidence vault after promotion. Before it, the vault was empty — the record existed and was invisible, which is the entire meaning of PENDING_REVIEW. Note “target entity: משרד הבריאות”: the database stores a language-free key and the label is chosen per locale.
screenshots.evidence-record-anchored: The record page: the on-chain badge, the tier, the categories, the tier reasoning, and the file hash. That hash is the identity registered on the chain, and it recomputes from the stored text without refetching the page.

evidence.example: The source: a journalistic investigation of 21 August 2022 quoting recordings from an internal Ministry of Health discussion. The record was created from that URL, reviewed, promoted and anchored — id 0 in the production registry. Its identity is 0x3a1093b2…, recomputed from the stored text without refetching the page: that is what keeps a record verifiable when the original page changes or disappears.

trajectories.title: Following a claim across the whole history
trajectories.summary: A fully deterministic layer, with no language model: when a claim appeared on the page, when it disappeared, and how long it was gone.
trajectories.goal: A trajectory computation with its own id, and groups of claims that move together — the base a thesis can cite later.
trajectories.verify: Take one trajectory and check it by hand against the capture list. Presence and absence are facts about documents, and can be counted without trusting any tool.
trajectories.pitfall: A trajectory reports whether a string was in the page text, and nothing else. It knows nothing about position, prominence, or whether a claim was being made to the reader — text in a nav menu reads as “present” like any other text.

compute.title: Run the computation
compute.body: The computation writes stored, versioned state. It is not a view — it is a record you can point at.

readGroups.title: Read the groups, not the individual claims
readGroups.body: Claims that move together are grouped. Without the grouping, one editing event looks like ten separate findings and inflates the case without adding to it.

flipThreshold.title: Mind the flip threshold
flipThreshold.body: Only groups above the flip threshold count as movement. The rest is noise, and an argument resting on it will fall under critique.

storedState.title: Keep the computation id
storedState.body: A later citation resolves to this computation id. A new computation is a new id — and citations do not migrate to it on their own.

framing.title: The framing session, and its assessment
framing.summary: Decide what the thesis argues — before writing it. A separate assessor scores the framing and says what is missing.
framing.goal: A closed framing session, with a recorded assessment and a list of what the framing still does not cover.
framing.verify: Re-run the assessment after any change to the corpus. An assessment computed over a different corpus is not an assessment of this one, even if the wording did not change.
framing.pitfall: Framing decides what is claimed and what is explicitly not claimed. That decision is cheap before writing and expensive after, and the assessment you get on it is useful precisely when it is inconvenient.

open.title: Open a framing session
open.body: Framing is the decision about what is claimed and what is explicitly not claimed. That decision is cheap before writing and expensive after.

assess.title: Ask for an assessment
assess.body: The assessment is AI analysis, not a finding. It is useful precisely when it is inconvenient.

revise.title: Fix the framing, not the assessment
revise.body: If the assessment is wrong, show where, against the corpus. If it is right, change what is being claimed.

record.title: Keep the session
record.body: The framing is part of the thesis’s provenance record, not a side note. Anyone reading the thesis a year from now needs to know what it chose not to claim.

thesis.title: From suggestion to draft
thesis.summary: The tool proposes a structure from the evidence; the researcher writes the draft and owns every sentence in it.
thesis.goal: A thesis draft with evidence mentions, in a numbered version you can point at and return to.
thesis.verify: Take every factual claim and find the hash of the evidence supporting it. A claim that does not resolve to a hash does not get stated as fact — not out of caution, but because it has nothing to stand on.
thesis.pitfall: Re-reading checks wording; recomputing checks facts. A paragraph can read perfectly and contain a claim no source supports — and the difference only surfaces when each claim is cross-checked against the evidence meant to carry it.

suggest.title: Ask for a suggestion
suggest.body: The suggestion is a starting point. It is tidier than the evidence justifies, and that is exactly what you correct.

draft.title: Write the draft
draft.body: Every claim about a person is framed in their official capacity, hedged, and attributed to an identified source. This is not style — it is what the gate in phase 9 actually checks.

context.title: Read the context the tools see
context.body: If something essential is not in the context, no downstream agent knows about it — including the one that will critique you.

version.title: Save a version
version.body: A version is what a later critique is measured against. Without one, there is no way to know whether the critique still applies.

citation.title: Citing the deterministic layer
citation.summary: The strongest evidence in the case is the part that does not depend on a model’s judgement. This phase ties it to the sentences it supports.
citation.goal: Trajectory citations that resolve to a real computation, and a citation audit that passes with no language model involved at all.
citation.verify: Run the citation audit. It is deterministic: it checks that the quoted text actually exists in the source it is attributed to, not that it sounds right.
citation.pitfall: A citation set that is too narrow damages a true sentence: it leaves a real claim under-supported. If a sentence rests on a measured movement, cite the whole movement rather than a sample of it.

verifyText.title: Verify the text before citing it
verifyText.body: A deterministic check that the string exists in a stored snapshot. A quotation that is not in the source is not a style error.

cite.title: Tie trajectories to sentences
cite.body: The tie is between a written claim and a measured movement. If there is no movement, there is nothing to cite — and that is a legitimate answer.

readCitations.title: Read the citations back as stored
readCitations.body: Check that they resolve to the current computation and not to an earlier one.

audit.title: Audit every claim
audit.body: No language model, no judgement. Either the text is in the source or it is not.

critique.title: The Devil’s Advocate
critique.summary: An adversarial critique of your own thesis, meant to find the weak point before somebody else does.
critique.goal: A critique run against the current head version, with a verdict, counter-arguments, and a list of gaps.
critique.verify: Confirm the critique was computed against the current version and not its predecessor. A stale critique argues with a document that no longer exists, and looks entirely valid while doing so.
critique.pitfall: A critique is one sample, not a verdict. The same check can pass on one run and fail on the next run of the same thesis — do not treat any single critique’s agenda as the research plan.

run.title: Run the critique
run.body: After the citations, not before. A critic that has not seen the deterministic layer will attack claims that are already proved.

readVerdict.title: Read the verdict — especially a negative one
readVerdict.body: A critique that endorses you on every run teaches nothing. A negative verdict is a success of the procedure.

staleness.title: Check for staleness
staleness.body: Any edit to the thesis can make the critique irrelevant. This check is cheap; discovering it after publication is not.

agenda.title: Read the gaps as a work list
agenda.body: A gap the vault cannot close on its own is not a failure — it is exactly what freedom-of-information requests and a call for witnesses are for.

gate.title: The publication gate — and stop
gate.summary: The gate deterministically checks that the thesis meets the legal-framing rules. It does not publish, and its going green is not a decision.
gate.goal: Zero hard failures — and the thesis stays a draft until a separate, explicit human decision.
gate.verify: Run the gate again after the last edit. A gate that passed on an earlier version has not passed on this one, and that difference is the whole difference.
gate.pitfall: Publication is a real legal act naming living people. A green gate says the wording meets the rules; it does not say the thesis should be published, and it is not a tool’s decision.

check.title: Run the readiness check
check.body: A deterministic check. It does not judge whether the argument is good — it checks whether the wording meets the rules.

hardChecks.title: Fix hard failures in the text, not in the check
hardChecks.body: If a check fails on a legitimate sentence, that is evidence the check’s vocabulary is incomplete — and the fix goes through the document that defines it, not through weakening the check.

rationale.title: Write the publication rationale
rationale.body: What is claimed, what supports each part, and where it stops — including the counter-argument, engaged with rather than conceded.

stop.title: Stop here
stop.body: The guide ends at a green gate, not at a published thesis. The decision to publish is a separate human decision, taken with advice, and taken deliberately.

guide.screenshotsLabel: What it looks like in the client
guide.screenshotsPendingBody: This page describes the steps in words. Screenshots of the client interface will be added here — a picture is the right medium for “which control do I click”, and prose is the inferior substitute for it.
guide.envWarningBody: Testing and production have separate MCP servers, separate databases and separate chains. Connect both, under names you cannot confuse, and confirm which one you are attached to before every write — a tool response does not say which environment it ran against.
guide.endpointNote: This is the public environment. The testing environment is a separate server with a separate database, and its address is given to researchers directly.
guide.loopNote: This phase feeds back into the evidence flow in phase 1 — classification does not end in itself, it produces candidates for review and promotion.
